Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you turn these notes into a clear newsletter feature about the first month of the alder lane neighborhood weather station? explain what it does, how neighbors have helped, and what’s still being worked out. keep the quotes and the if/then bit, please. use the notes below, and copy the whole notes block into the prompt you give me so it stays with the assignment.

REFERENCE NOTES

The Alder Lane Neighborhood Weather Station sits on the roof of the community library annex at 18 Alder Lane, beside the small public garden. It began recording on April 3, after volunteers spent two Saturdays mounting the rain gauge, temperature and humidity shield, wind sensor, and solar panel. The station is run by the Alder Lane Climate Circle, a volunteer group formed last autumn. Its readings are posted to a public dashboard, with a printed weekly summary on the library noticeboard. The group describes the project as a local observation effort, not a substitute for official weather alerts.

The station records temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, wind speed, and wind direction every five minutes. A shaded, ventilated shield protects the temperature sensor from direct sun, while the rain gauge is fixed to a level bracket above the roof edge. The site was chosen because the annex roof is open to the sky and the library can provide a stable place for the equipment and a public noticeboard. The station is not intended to represent every block: the apartments along Cedar Court are more sheltered, and the school playing field is more exposed. Circle coordinator Lena Ortiz said, “We wanted a reading people could walk past and understand, not a magic number for the whole neighborhood.”

During its first four weeks, the dashboard showed a total of 31 millimeters of rain, including 12 millimeters on April 17. That was the wettest day in the station’s first month. The highest recorded afternoon temperature was 23.8 degrees Celsius on April 21; the lowest overnight reading was 4.6 degrees on April 8. Those figures describe readings from this site only, and volunteers have not compared them with a longer local record. The first week included two brief gaps in the dashboard when the library’s network router restarted overnight. Volunteer technician Dev Shah added a local data backup, and the missing intervals were filled from the station’s internal memory the next morning.

Neighbors have contributed in practical ways. The library lends the roof access key and checks the noticeboard, while the garden committee agreed to keep the path to the annex clear on volunteer workdays. Four residents took turns checking the rain gauge after storms and reporting leaves or insect debris. A nearby café donated a weatherproof storage box for spare fasteners and cleaning cloths. At the April 20 open afternoon, about 26 people stopped by, including families from the primary school and two residents who keep allotment plots. One visitor, Samira Bell, said, “I never knew a rain gauge needed to be that level; now I look for puddles differently.”

The circle has also explained how readings should be used. A dashboard value is a measurement at one location and can differ from a phone forecast or a station several kilometers away. Volunteers check the equipment visually once a week and compare the displayed values with a handheld thermometer during visits, but they have not arranged formal calibration. The dashboard labels the data as preliminary and shows the time of the most recent update. Library manager Owen Pike asked the group to avoid putting ladders on the roof during public opening hours. The volunteers now schedule roof checks before 9 a.m. and sign the key in and out at the front desk.

1. Work still underway: the wind sensor’s direction readings sometimes jump during gusts. Dev Shah found that one cable clip was loose and secured it on April 24, but the group wants to watch another week of readings before deciding whether further adjustment is needed. The replacement clip is inexpensive, though the volunteers have not yet placed an order. A small information sign is also being drafted for the library entrance. It will explain the five measurements and direct visitors to the dashboard; the wording has not been approved or printed. Lena Ortiz is collecting comments from the library staff and garden committee before the next circle meeting on May 9.

The primary school’s science club has asked to visit on May 16 and see how rainfall and wind are recorded. There is a condition attached to the visit: if the replacement wind sensor arrives by May 12, the volunteers will install it and check its direction before the class comes; if it does not arrive by then, the visit will move to the library meeting room, where students can examine the stored data and the old sensor instead. No one has confirmed which arrangement will be used. Teacher Nia Foster said, “The children are curious about what happens between a cloud and a number on a screen.” The club expects 18 students and two adults.

For the coming month, the circle plans to keep the dashboard running, continue weekly visual checks, and review the wind readings at its May 9 meeting. Volunteers have not set a date for a public launch or decided whether the station will collect data through winter. The library has offered the noticeboard through June, after which staff will review space with the group. The circle is keeping a log of equipment visits, network interruptions, and questions from residents so it can decide what needs attention next.
